title: LRIM: Physics-Based Benchmark for Long-Range Graph Learning
one_liner: Graph models claim to see far away but actually rely on nearby neighbors; this paper proves it by building a physics-based test where distant parts MUST talk to each other.
lead: Graph models process data arranged in networks—like molecules with atoms connected by bonds, or social networks with people connected by friendships. They work by passing messages between neighboring nodes. The question everyone asks: can a model see far away across the graph, or does it get stuck in the immediate neighborhood? Existing benchmarks cannot truly prove the answer. This paper uses the Ising model, a physics system where distant parts genuinely depend on each other, to build the first benchmark that provably requires long-range vision.

problem.h2: How do you know if a graph model truly sees far away?
paras: Graph neural networks work by passing information between neighbors, like whispering down a line. To see something far away, the message must hop through many intermediate nodes. But here's the trap: a node might get the right answer by accident, using only nearby neighbors and ignoring distant ones. If all your test problems happen to be solvable by local information, you'll never catch the cheating.

Existing benchmarks suffer from this flaw. A model that claims to 'see 100 hops away' might just be picking up patterns in the neighborhoods, not truly integrating distant signals. There's no way to guarantee that long-range vision actually matters for the task.

callout.html: You need a test where the right answer is mathematically impossible without information from far away.

panels.title: 1. The neighborhood trap
panels.caption: A node sees only nearby neighbors; far nodes are invisible.

panels.title: 2. Old benchmarks fail
panels.caption: Existing tests don't prove whether you need distant information.

panels.title: 3. Physics knows better
panels.caption: In the Ising model, distant atoms force each other to align.

panels.title: 4. LRIM builds the proof
panels.caption: The Ising model's solution provably depends on seeing far.

panels.title: 5. Models fail the test
panels.caption: Most models stay stuck; only those with true long-range vision pass.

steps.text: Choose a grid of magnetic atoms with tunable coupling strength.
Calculate what the atoms do when fully relaxed, which depends on distant interactions.
Turn atoms into nodes, connections into edges, add node features based on local context.
Can the graph model recover the ground truth configuration using only the local features?
Vary graph size (256 to 65k nodes) and coupling strength to control how far apart atoms must 'talk'.

paras: The paper does not change a model architecture or training method. Instead, it changes the TEST itself. LRIM swaps out vague benchmarks for a physics-grounded one where you can mathematically prove whether long-range information is actually necessary.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: degree of long-range coupling
hidden.name: coupling strength (how far atoms influence each other)
paras: In the Ising model, atoms exert magnetic force on their neighbors. At low coupling, only nearby atoms matter. At high coupling, distant atoms start to influence the outcome. The coupling strength is a dial: turn it down and the problem becomes local, turn it up and you must see far.

LRIM measures this by computing the ground truth (the relaxed state of the model) at each coupling level. A graph model's accuracy directly reflects how well it can capture long-range dependencies: weak accuracy at high coupling shows the model is stuck in local neighborhoods.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger coupling; information must travel farther. Highlighted cells require true long-range vision.

reads.html: The coupling strength is a number you can dial up or down. At high settings, atoms far apart force each other to align. A model predicting the outcome must see those distant forces.
The Ising model ground state is proven to depend on coupling; tuning the coupling dial lets LRIM create tasks of controllable long-rangedness.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: physics proves the necessity
paras: The Ising model is a classical physics system with a proven ground state (the lowest-energy configuration). Mathematicians have solved it completely. When you increase coupling, distant atoms genuinely influence the ground state—there is no way to get the right answer without seeing far. This is not a guess from data; it is mathematical proof.

By asking a graph model to predict the Ising ground state, LRIM forces it to either learn long-range vision or fail. The model cannot cheat by memorizing local patterns. If it stays at chance performance when coupling is high, it proves the model is blind to distant information. If it succeeds, it demonstrates genuine long-range capability.

stages.s: Local node features from Ising atoms
Messages hop across the graph to distant nodes
Integrate distant signals into node predictions
Final node state matching Ising ground truth

math.h2: The Ising model ground state energy
math.words: Total energy equals negative coupling strength times the number of aligned neighbor pairs, minus external field times each atom's state.
symbols: the state of atom i, either spin-up or spin-down

worked.title: A tiny worked example with 4 atoms in a line
lines: Grid: atom1-atom2-atom3-atom4, coupling J=2.0, field B=0.
All-up is lower energy (-6.0 vs 2.0), so ground state has all atoms aligned.
Atoms far apart (atom1 and atom4) still both align up, even though not direct neighbors—this is long-range coupling in action.

math.note: The model must predict each atom's spin by integrating the coupling pattern, which forces information to travel across the entire graph.

bars.h2: How models fare at different coupling strengths

charts.title: Local message-passing only
charts.note: Accuracy crashes when atoms must align across the graph.

charts.title: Graph transformer (attends to all nodes)
charts.note: Better than local models because it can attend to distant nodes, but accuracy still falls at high coupling because computing all-to-all comparisons for 65k nodes becomes computationally intractable, so the model uses approximations that lose information.

items.html: Storing connections between all pairs of 65k nodes requires a lot of graphics-card memory. Models designed to skip these connections often sacrifice accuracy.
Real graphs (molecules, social networks) have different structures and noise. A model that solves LRIM might still struggle on messy real data.

items.b: Tuning coupling by hand is brittle.
items.html: If coupling is set wrong, the task might accidentally become solvable by local information, hiding the model's weakness.

items.b: Done right: a true long-range model passes all coupling levels.
items.html: If a model maintains high accuracy across weak and strong coupling, you know it genuinely integrates distant information, not just memorizing local patterns.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple graph neural network (2-3 layers of message-passing) and a graph transformer variant. Run both on LRIM with three coupling strengths: weak, medium, and strong. Plot accuracy as coupling increases. A genuine long-range model should stay flat; a local-only model should crash at high coupling.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = (number of correctly predicted spins) / (total spins)
demo.closing: The shape of the accuracy curve—not the absolute number—reveals whether the model can actually see far.
